Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Arjun’s captivity began on a crisp autumn morning when two uniformed officers escorted him from his South Asian-American home into a windowless holding room. He remained there for days, watched constantly by figures in crisp uniforms who moved with purpose and spoke in measured tones. He remembered the event not as a long stretch of time but as a series of sharp pictures: the gleam of brass buttons, the sudden drop of a metal tray, the tightness across his ribs where restraints had dug in. Each moment hung like a photograph in his mind. When the memory surfaces now, the dull ache in his left knee and the tight band across his chest return instantly, mirroring the exact places where the restraints had pressed. Sometimes, however, he watches those same images unfold and feels completely numb, as if observing a man in a photograph while his own body remains quiet. In the weeks that followed, Arjun found himself moving through familiar rooms like a stranger. He began restricting his eating to exact portions, watching the clock and measuring each bite. When his partner, Maya, reached for his hand or asked which restaurant he preferred, he nodded and agreed without hesitation, going along with whatever they wanted. These revenge fantasies played out behind his eyes during long drives, replaying scenarios where he corrected the mistakes of the men who had held him, while his strict eating routines and quiet people pleasing settled alongside them. His symptom inventory, hovering at forty, mirrored this steady accumulation. He had come to believe that the world outside his routines remained fundamentally unpredictable, a certainty that settled deep in his chest. As a park ranger at Crestwood National Preserve, his daily environment brought these habits into constant contact with the outdoors and the people who visit. The ranger station’s open desk meant visitors constantly paused to watch him stamp permits, and Arjun was acutely aware of being seen. When a visitor began talking about their brother’s deployment or the military’s latest operations, his jaw tightened; the familiar weight of the holding room returned. He kept listening, but his attention drifted to the door, bracing for movement. One afternoon, while patrolling the northern ridge, a deer bolted from the brush and a uniformed park warden stepped from behind a pine. Arjun’s body snapped toward them, heart racing, startled as if the ground itself were shifting beneath him. Even when Maya assured him he was home and the woods were quiet, he found it impossible to believe it. Safety felt like a promise others kept, not a reality he could rest in. Over months, the quiet isolation deepened. He felt isolated and set apart from the seasonal rangers. The humiliation of the holding room lingered like a second uniform, never quite shed. He compared himself to the other men on the trail, certain the constant scrutiny and the way his knees still ached ran parallel to his self-comparison. When Maya suggested they attend a community picnic, he went, nodding at every passing authority figure, his meals measured, his eyes tracking every shift in the crowd. The habit of watching and yielding became a steady rhythm, changing how he worked and related without demanding explanation. What finally brought Arjun to seek help was not a single crisis but a gradual tightening: the way he stopped finishing conversations when military topics arose, the way his body flinched before his mind could register a movement, the quiet certainty that the world outside his routines remained unpredictable. He hopes for a space where he can stop measuring every breath and every glance, where the images of the holding room can settle without pulling his ribs taut. Most of all, he wants to believe that safety can be trusted, even when it looks exactly like it didn’t matter before.
